learningObjective: Explain the role of a Device Mesh as a logical named-axis grid decoupled from the physical topology.

canonicalClaims.claim: A Device Mesh assigns each device in a group to a coordinate in a multi-dimensional grid with named axes (e.g. 'data', 'model'), and sharding specifications refer to those axis names; the mapping to physical devices is a separate concern that the compiler / runtime resolves.
conditions: The mesh is rectangular (or a product of axes); every axis has a size.
Sharding annotations reference mesh axes by name, not by rank id.
nonImplications: Does not imply that the mesh must match the physical topology; the runtime is free to permute the assignment to optimize link usage.
Does not imply that a 2D mesh 'data × model' fixes the axis of parallelism — the same tensor can be sharded along any axis via its sharding spec.

misconceptions.claim: The Device Mesh directly assigns each rank to a physical GPU; changing mesh axes requires recabling the cluster.
misconceptions.whyWrong: The mesh is a logical abstraction; the runtime maps mesh coordinates to physical devices, and can choose different mappings for different jobs.

misconceptions.claim: A 2D mesh named ('data', 'model') forces the compiler to shard batch on 'data' and weights on 'model'; sharding cannot cross axes.
misconceptions.whyWrong: The names are just axis labels; sharding specs decide which axes each tensor is sharded on, and a single tensor may be sharded on multiple axes.

misconceptions.claim: The Device Mesh is a NCCL-specific concept and is not part of the compiler IR.
misconceptions.whyWrong: The mesh (and named axes) is a first-class concept in GSPMD / XLA / StableHLO sharding, exposed in the IR to drive partitioning decisions.
